abstract: |
  Response bias can mean an observed tendency to respond "yes" or the location of a criterion on a latent evidence scale. The standard index, c, measures the second under an equal-variance Gaussian model. I develop a reporting convention for the first: PPB (Positive Predictive Bias), the sum of the hit and false alarm rates, paired with Youden's J, their difference. PPB is twice Macmillan and Creelman’s (1990) yes rate, which they rated favorably on every pragmatic criterion, although they preferred c for consistency with d′. For interior rates, PPB corresponds to criterion location under an equal-variance uniform model. Because it is linear in the rates, PPB, unlike c, is defined at rates of 0 or 1, is unbiased, averages exactly across observers, and expresses covariate effects in probability units. In the configurations tested, boundary corrections biased c by up to 0.12, and the mean of individual c values differed from c at the mean rates by nearly half the latter’s magnitude. For sparse counts, I construct a conservative confidence interval with guaranteed binomial coverage and a narrower approximate interval. In eyewitness data, 62% of participants had a rate of 0 or 1 (Colloff et al., 2022); in three experiments with one trial per type, c was undefined for every participant, while PPB showed that showups raised identification probability, averaged across target-present and target-absent trials, by 5 to 19 percentage points relative to simultaneous showups (Colloff & Wixted, 2020).

# Introduction

Two problems recur when researchers seek to distinguish response bias—the tendency to favor one response—from classification accuracy. First, the criterion measure $c$ becomes undefined when either response rate equals 0 or 1, which is common when observers complete few trials or respond accurately. For example, participants in the eyewitness lineup study by Colloff et al. [-@colloff_active_2022] completed only four target-present (signal) and four target-absent (noise) lineup trials each. Since most eyewitness experiments test each witness once [@mickes_receiver_2012], $c$ often cannot be computed for individual witnesses at all.

The second problem is conceptual. Researchers often describe $c$ as a measure of the tendency to respond "yes" or "no." Yet, more precisely, it locates the decision criterion: the evidence value above which an observer responds "yes" on an unobserved evidence scale. While these two readings do coincide at fixed $d'$ under the assumption of Gaussian distributions, they diverge when $d'$ varies or the distributions differ. Many applied researchers work directly with the two observed rates or simple functions of them [@rotello_when_2015], and so lack a summary measure of response bias that can be interpreted directly from the observed rates.

Positive Predictive Bias (PPB), defined as the true positive rate (TPR, or hit rate $H$) plus the false positive rate (FPR, or false alarm rate $F$), addresses both problems. It complements Youden's $J = \text{TPR} - \text{FPR}$ [@youden_index_1950; @peirce_numerical_1884] in the same way that $c$ complements $d'$. In geometric terms, $J$ and PPB are perpendicular contrasts of the same two rates: whereas $J$ summarizes accuracy, PPB summarizes response bias.

@macmillan_response_1990 [p. 409] classify bias indexes according to both their assumed latent distributions and their target parameters. The decision criterion is the threshold on an observer’s internal evidence scale above which they respond "yes." Under the equal-variance uniform model, TPR + FPR is linearly related to this threshold’s position relative to the midpoint of the two evidence distributions. With equal numbers of signal and noise trials, $(H + F)/2$ is the proportion of "yes" responses, which Macmillan and Creelman call the yes rate [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]. They investigate the yes rate against other bias indexes on key measurement properties: monotonic constant-bias (isobias) curves that behave sensibly at and below chance, range independence (parallel isobias curves on some coordinates), pooling across observers without distortion (aggregation), so that the index computed from a group's mean rates equals the mean of the individual indexes, and a known sampling distribution. The yes rate is the only index rated positively on all six pragmatic criteria in their Table 2 [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 412]; $c$, by contrast, is rated marginal for aggregation, since pooling observers who differ in accuracy distorts the metric (Table 2, p. 412).

Despite this, Macmillan and Creelman argue for preferring $c$ to the yes rate [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 411], on the principle that the bias index should come from the same model as the sensitivity index, while concluding that criterion-location indexes, the yes rate included, are the best bias statistics (p. 412). Their argument rests on the same-model principle and on the superiority of normal and logistic models to rectangular ones on the basis of ROC predictions (p. 411); with $d'$ as the sensitivity index of the normal model, $c$ is its bias index. However, when accuracy is measured by $J$ rather than $d'$, the same principle just as well favors the yes rate. Nonetheless, $c$ has prevailed: calculation guides and software present $c$, $\beta$, and $B''$ [@stanislaw_calculation_1999], while the yes rate has received little further attention.

This article reconsiders the yes rate as PPB. Exact unbiasedness under binomial sampling and exact aggregation are shared by fixed linear combinations of the two rates. PPB uses their sum, $H+F$, because it represents twice the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation without assumptions about latent evidence distributions, and forms a perpendicular contrast to $J$. The contribution is a reporting convention for this established quantity, paired with $J$. PPB is also defined at boundary rates, and covariate effects on it are expressed in probability units. I quantify these properties where boundary rates are common, with 10 to 20 trials of each type per observer and accurate responding, in an eyewitness dataset with four trials of each type, and in three eyewitness experiments with one trial of each type. I also assess whether PPB and $c$ remain stable when experimental changes make signal and noise easier or harder to distinguish in two recognition-memory datasets. Finally, I identify the settings in which $c$ remains preferable.

# Definition and Properties

Consider an observer with rates $H$ and $F$, estimated from $n_s$ signal trials and $n_n$ noise trials. PPB is defined as

$$\text{PPB} = H + F$$ {#eq-ppb}

PPB is twice the yes rate of Macmillan and Creelman [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]; doubling places balanced response propensity at 1 and simplifies @eq-inverse. Values above 1 indicate liberal responding, and values below 1 conservative responding, relative to equal presentation of the two trial types. PPB is distinct from positive predictive value, the proportion of positive responses that are correct. With signal probability $\pi$, the overall proportion of "yes" responses is $\pi H + (1 - \pi)F$, which equals PPB/2 when $\pi = 1/2$. The criterion interpretation below (@eq-crect) uses rates within each trial type and does not require $\pi = 1/2$ (Supplement §1.4). Response tendency has consequences apart from accuracy: liberal responding by an eyewitness means more identifications of innocent suspects [@wells_eyewitness_2003], conservative responding by a radiologist may miss cancers, and radiologists reading the same mammograms differ several-fold in false positive rate [@elmore_screening_2002].

Youden's $J = H - F$ measures accuracy in the observed rates, as $d'$ measures discriminability on the latent scale under equal-variance Gaussian signal detection theory (EVSDT). $J$ and PPB form a perpendicular pair of contrasts on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) unit square (@fig-roc, Panel A):

$$H = \frac{J + \text{PPB}}{2}, \qquad F = \frac{\text{PPB} - J}{2}$$ {#eq-inverse}

Because both rates lie in $[0, 1]$, @eq-inverse implies the joint range $|J| \le \text{PPB} \le 2 - |J|$, a diamond in the $(J, \text{PPB})$ plane. PPB spans its full range, $[0, 2]$, only when $J = 0$; when $J = 0.87$, PPB must lie between 0.87 and 1.13. A raw PPB difference therefore represents a larger share of the available range in the more accurate group. These bounds concern attainable values at fixed observed $J$, not Macmillan and Creelman's range independence [-@macmillan_response_1990, pp. 409, 411]. Perpendicular contrasts are also not statistically independent: for fixed trial counts, the sampling covariance of PPB and $J$ is $\operatorname{Var}(\hat H) - \operatorname{Var}(\hat F)$ (Supplement §5).

By linearity, $\widehat{\text{PPB}}$ is exactly unbiased for PPB at every combination of $n_s$, $n_n$, $H$, and $F$, and independence between the two trial types gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\text{PPB}}) = \frac{H(1 - H)}{n_s} + \frac{F(1 - F)}{n_n}$$ {#eq-variance}

For observers with few trials, I construct a conservative interval by adding the lower bounds of the Clopper--Pearson intervals for $H$ and $F$ and, separately, their upper bounds, each at confidence level $1 - \alpha/2$ [@clopper_use_1934]; the sum covers PPB with probability at least $1 - \alpha$ under binomial sampling, boundary observations included. The plug-in normal-approximation interval can under-cover or collapse to zero width with sparse counts. A narrower adjusted interval, Agresti and Caffo's [-@agresti_simple_2000] interval for $H - (1 - F)$ shifted by one, has no coverage guarantee, so I examine its coverage by enumeration. Population means and paired condition differences need uncertainty across participants instead (Supplement §5).

Under EVSDT, $(d', c)$ are the corresponding contrasts of probit-transformed rates (zROC space):

$$d' = z(H) - z(F), \qquad -2c = z(H) + z(F)$$ {#eq-sdt}

Here $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard-normal cumulative distribution and density functions, and $z = \Phi^{-1}$. With noise and signal evidence Gaussian with unit variance and means 0 and $d'$, $H = \Phi(d'/2 - c)$ and $F = \Phi(-d'/2 - c)$, so $c$ locates the criterion relative to the midpoint between the two means (Supplement §1.2). Because $\Phi$ is increasing, PPB decreases in $c$ at fixed $d'$:

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial c} = -\left[\phi(d'/2 - c) + \phi(-d'/2 - c)\right] < 0$$ {#eq-monotone}

PPB and $c$ therefore rank observers consistently whenever $\Delta H$ and $\Delta F$ have the same sign: for any strictly increasing link $g$, $\Delta g(H) + \Delta g(F)$ then shares the sign of $\Delta H + \Delta F$, so every link-based criterion agrees with PPB. Divergent rankings require the rates to move in opposite directions, $|\Delta J| > |\Delta \text{PPB}|$, a necessary but not sufficient condition that is typical when groups differ in accuracy. Matching groups on PPB does not match their accuracy.

Interpreting PPB as criterion location, like interpreting $c$, invokes a model. Suppose that noise evidence is uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$ and signal evidence on $[\delta, 1 + \delta]$. When the criterion $\theta$ lies within both distributions, $F = 1 - \theta$ and $H = 1 - \theta + \delta$, so $\delta = J$. Measured from the midpoint of the two distribution means, the criterion is

$$c_{\text{rect}} = \theta - \frac{1 + \delta}{2} = \frac{1 - \text{PPB}}{2}$$ {#eq-crect}

@eq-crect is Macmillan and Creelman's $k = 0.5[1 - (F + H)]$ [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]. Their paired sensitivity parameter is $H - F = J$, which Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] call $P_r$. The criterion expression does not involve discriminability: observers who place the criterion at the same position relative to the midpoint have the same PPB at every $J$, in parallel with the independence of $c$ from $d'$ under EVSDT. The relation holds when the criterion lies in the distributions' overlap, endpoints included; outside it, the affine formula need not recover criterion location, while PPB retains its yes-rate interpretation (Supplement §1.4). The uniform model implies a straight interior ROC segment of unit slope, with additional segments along the edges of the ROC square. Empirical ROC curves generally contradict this shape, so I use it to say what PPB measures when it holds, not as a model of any dataset. Equivalently, in the generalized linear model form of signal detection theory [@decarlo_signal_1998], where $d'$ is the difference of link-transformed rates and the criterion is their sum, up to scale, replacing the probit with the identity link centered on balanced response propensity, $z(p) = p - \frac{1}{2}$, yields $J$ and $(1 - \text{PPB})/2$ (Supplement §1.4).

The nonparametric indexes $B''$ [@grier_nonparametric_1971] and $B''_D$ [@donaldson_measuring_1992], built from products and ratios of the two rates, do not generally aggregate exactly (see Aggregation). $B''$ must also be reversed by hand for below-chance performance ($H < F$) [@grier_nonparametric_1971], whereas PPB remains continuous there and keeps its yes-rate interpretation. Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] pair $J$ with $B_r = F/(1 - J)$, the probability of responding "yes" from an uncertain evidence state under the same model as PPB; it is equivalent to Macmillan and Creelman's error ratio $k'$ [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406], and its denominator is zero at $H = 1$ and $F = 0$. $B_r$ normalizes criterion location by the width of the uncertain region, as $c'$ normalizes $c$ by $d'$, so for fixed $0 \le J < 1$ it spans $[0, 1]$. Curves of constant yes rate are parallel, whereas curves of constant error ratio radiate from a common point, so the two indexes can rank observers with different levels of accuracy differently.

Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] test this distinction on the principle that a bias index should remain invariant under manipulations of discriminability, and a discrimination index under manipulations of bias. In a $2 \times 3$ within-subjects design crossing word imagery with three payoff matrices (different rewards and penalties for correct responses and errors), a valid bias index should track the payoff manipulation, remain stable across imagery conditions, and show a similar payoff effect in each imagery condition. The pair $(J, B_r)$ and the criterion indexes of the normal and logistic models pass; $\ln \beta$, $B''$, and $B'_H$ fail on the interaction. Snodgrass and Corwin did not test the yes rate as an index, although they report $H$ and $F$ separately.

An evidence model does not specify how observers set the criterion as discriminability changes: they might keep its position relative to the midpoint or keep the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation, and which rule they follow is an empirical question. Studies of recognition memory find that observers often keep a criterion fixed when item strength changes, at least within a test list [@stretch_difference_1998; @verde_memory_2007]. Under EVSDT, an observer who maintains $c = -0.5$ has $(H, F) = (0.84, 0.50)$ at $d' = 1$ and $(H, F) = (0.93, 0.31)$ at $d' = 2$. PPB consequently falls from 1.34 to 1.24 while $c$ remains constant. Under double high-threshold theory, the result depends on which of the model's two bias parameters is held fixed: a constant $c_{\text{rect}}$ produces the same PPB at every $J$, whereas a constant guess rate of $B_r = 0.40$ raises PPB from 0.86 to 0.92 as $J$ increases from 0.3 to 0.6.

Under EVSDT the probit inverts the distribution function that generated the rates, so $c$ recovers criterion location; with non-Gaussian latent distributions it need not (Supplement §1.3). PPB’s interpretation as twice the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation requires no assumptions about latent evidence distributions, whereas $c$’s criterion interpretation requires EVSDT. This distinction concerns the reporting target and model assumptions; the estimators can also differ in finite-sample bias and uncertainty.

The rest of the paper puts numbers to these claims: how much bias the boundary corrections add at the trial counts of applied work, how covariate effects differ between probability and criterion units, how far two criterion summaries of a group (the mean of individual $c$ values and $c$ at the mean rates) diverge, and how often the two decompositions rank groups differently.

# Methods

## Analysis design

The boundary-stability analysis is an exact calculation and the other original analyses are simulations; their reported trial counts are totals split equally between signal and noise trials. A separate interval analysis enumerates binomial outcomes at four, ten, and twenty trials per class, including unequal denominators, across a grid of operating points (pairs of hit and false alarm rates; Supplement §5). Two further simulations, of groups with similar PPB and different accuracy, are in Supplement §7. The supplement gives the derivations.

Four analyses evaluate three practical properties of PPB: boundary stability, the units of covariate effects, and exact aggregation. The boundary-stability analysis used four configurations chosen so that boundary estimates would be common: $(H, F, n)$ = $(0.80, 0.05, 20)$, $(0.95, 0.20, 20)$, $(0.95, 0.05, 20)$, and $(0.95, 0.10, 40)$. For each, I computed the exact expected bias of PPB and of $c$ after either the log-linear correction [@hautus_corrections_1995] or the $1/2N$ correction [see @macmillan_detection_1985] by enumerating every binomial outcome. The regression simulation assigned the same logit-scale bias coefficient ($\beta = 0.3$) to two accuracy groups and compared their estimated slopes (2,000 subjects per group, 40 trials per subject). The aggregation simulation drew individual rates from beta distributions under three parameter settings. For PPB, $c$, $B''$, $B''_D$, and $B_r$, it compared the mean of 100 individual estimates with the estimate computed from the mean rates over 2,000 replications. Finally, a follow-up simulation examined the effects of applying corrections before aggregation and of excluding subjects whose estimated rates reached a boundary.

## Data

In addition to the simulations, I reanalyzed Experiment 1 from Colloff et al. [-@colloff_active_2022], a public eyewitness lineup dataset distributed in the pyWitness repository ([github.com/lmickes/pyWitness](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness); @mickes_pywitness_2024). The study included 220 participants, each of whom judged own-race lineups (faces from their own racial group) and other-race lineups (faces from another racial group). Each participant made eight decisions: four for target-present lineups and four for target-absent lineups. The present analysis pools across the interactive and static lineup conditions because that manipulation was crossed independently with the comparisons of interest.

The response in the primary analysis is choosing someone versus rejecting the lineup. Here, $H$ is the proportion of target-present trials on which any lineup member was chosen, whether the perpetrator or an innocent member (foil). $F$ is the proportion of target-absent trials on which any lineup member was chosen. Rejections are negative responses in both trial types. Here $J$ measures the separation between target-present and target-absent choosing rates; it does not measure correct culprit identification. I computed PPB, $c$ (uncorrected and with each correction), $B''$, and $B_r$ for each participant overall and separately for their own-race and other-race lineups. The subject-level analysis pooled the race conditions, yielding four signal and four noise trials for each of 220 participants. The condition-level analysis separated own-race and other-race lineups, yielding two trials of each type in each of 440 participant-by-condition observations. The own-race contrast uses a t-based confidence interval for the mean within-participant difference, rather than treating trials as independent observations.

As a sensitivity check, I used perpetrator-only coding for $H$, defining it as the proportion of all target-present trials on which the perpetrator was correctly identified. Choices of innocent lineup members counted as negative responses and remained in the denominator. $F$ remained the rate of choosing any lineup member in target-absent lineups. This perpetrator-only rate sum combines different response definitions across trial types and cannot be interpreted as twice the choosing probability. It is also distinct from the original study's suspect-identification ROC convention, which estimates innocent-suspect identifications by dividing target-absent foil identifications by lineup size [@colloff_active_2022]. The supplement gives the response mapping, category counts, and both analyses (Supplement §6).

I also reanalyzed Experiments 1 to 3 of Colloff and Wixted [-@colloff_why_2020], in which each participant made one target-present and one target-absent decision in a single identification condition. I compared the showup condition with the simultaneous-showup condition on participant-level PPB, $J$, and log-linear $c$, using Welch intervals. I omitted the standard-lineup condition of Experiment 3, because a positive response there includes choosing a filler (Supplement §8).

For Snodgrass and Corwin's test I used Experiments 1 and 2 of Layher et al. [-@layher_who_2020], with 1,000 trials per participant and cell, and the Measuring Memory Project [@starns_assessing_2019], with 100 per participant. In these reanalyses, memory strength was manipulated by varying the number of times each face or word was studied. I computed PPB and $J$ from raw rates and $c$ from log-linear corrected rates and tested each by two-way analysis of variance. I use Snodgrass and Corwin’s ANOVA criteria as a descriptive check and report differences between the strongest and weakest study conditions, with confidence intervals for each comparison.

# Results

## Boundary stability

PPB is defined throughout $[0, 1]^2$, including the boundaries. By contrast, the probit transformation for $c$ diverges at 0 and 1, so an observer with either rate at 0 or 1 requires a correction before the metric can be calculated. The standard log-linear [@hautus_corrections_1995] and $1/2N$ [see @macmillan_detection_1985] corrections yield different estimates and introduce systematic bias.

Across configurations in which 44\% to 84\% of subjects produced a boundary estimate, PPB remained unbiased. Both corrections left $c$ nearly unbiased only in the configuration with $F = 1 - H$ ($H = 0.95$, $F = 0.05$), in which the corrections to the two rates canceled. In the other three configurations, the log-linear correction yielded bias of as much as 0.10, and the $1/2N$ correction produced greater bias, reaching 0.12 (@fig-advantages, Panel A). Because bias in $c$ is measured in $z$ units, its relative magnitude provides the most informative comparison: the corrections attenuated the population value of $c$ by 17\% to 31\% in configurations where $c$ differed from zero.

## Covariate effects in probability units

Applied researchers routinely relate detection and false positive rates to covariates, as in studies of how radiologists' interpretive performance and false positive rates vary with their characteristics [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007; @elmore_screening_2002] and of how partisanship and reflection shift response bias in judging news as true or false [@batailler_signal_2022]. When $H$ and $F$ are modeled separately, predicted PPB is predicted $H$ plus predicted $F$, so a covariate's effect on bias is the sum of its effects in the two models, in probability units, whatever link those models use. The same additivity holds for $c$ on the $z$ scale, but unless the rate models use the probit link, each term must first be rescaled by $1/\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\cdot))$ before it corresponds to the rate models' effects (Supplement §4).

A single coefficient on the logit scale can produce different probability-scale effects at different positions in ROC space. Using criterion units is appropriate when the target is latent criterion location and EVSDT holds: under that model, a constant criterion shift changes $z(H)$ and $z(F)$ by a constant amount, and the probit removes probability-scale variation that reflects only the shape of the Gaussian distribution. When the research question concerns how much a covariate changes the probability of a "yes" response, probability-scale variation is the target. Effects in the two units describe different quantities; neither scale generally supplies a correction to the other.

In the regression simulation, the same logit-scale bias coefficient produced a PPB slope of 0.040 among high-accuracy observers and 0.119 among moderate-accuracy observers, a threefold difference. The corresponding slopes for $c$ differed by a factor of 1.6 (@fig-advantages, Panel C). In addition, 794 of the 2,000 high-accuracy subjects required a correction before $c$ could be computed. A constant logit-scale coefficient produces different changes in response probability at different baseline rates. The slope ratios illustrate how that same logit-scale change is expressed on the probability and probit scales.

## Uncertainty with sparse counts

At the four boundary-analysis operating points, nominal 95% normal-approximation coverage ranged from 85.76% to 98.62%. The simultaneous Clopper--Pearson sum interval guarantees at least nominal coverage under binomial sampling, but is wider: at $H=0.80$, $F=0.05$, and ten trials per class, expected widths were 0.973 for the simultaneous interval and 0.507 for the normal-approximation interval. Across the supplementary grid, the minimum simultaneous coverage was 99.36%, reflecting its conservatism (Supplement §5). The adjusted interval had expected width 0.597 at that operating point. Across the grid its coverage averaged 97.2% with a minimum of 91.5% and fell below 94% in 8.4% of configurations, and its mean expected width was 0.645, against 1.024 for the simultaneous interval. The normal-approximation interval averaged 75.4% coverage, with a minimum of 7.7%.

For these individual binomial intervals, I did not evaluate bootstrap or Bayesian methods, or exact-test inversion. Ordinary nonparametric resampling of an individual’s trials within each trial type leaves a boundary rate unchanged, yielding a zero-width percentile interval for that component. Participant-level bootstrap inference for population means or paired differences instead resamples whole participants and retains their paired measurements. A model-based bootstrap simulates responses from a fitted model, whose assumptions and estimates determine its behavior. A Bayesian interval depends on the prior and carries no frequentist coverage guarantee. Inverting an exact test for $H + F$ is possible and left for future work. Reporting the guaranteed and the adjusted intervals together is the practical answer: the first guarantees nominal coverage, and the second is narrower without that guarantee.

## A design with one trial of each type

In Experiments 1 to 3 of Colloff and Wixted [-@colloff_why_2020], each participant made one target-present and one target-absent decision, either after viewing a single face (showup) or after viewing that face among five similar faces while judging only the highlighted one (simultaneous showup). Every participant therefore has $H_i$ and $F_i$ equal to 0 or 1, and $c$ is undefined for all of them. With one trial of each type, the $1/2N$ correction moves every rate to 1/2 and returns $c = 0$ for every participant, and excluding boundary participants leaves no data. PPB needs no correction. Showups raised PPB relative to simultaneous showups by 0.102 (95% CI: 0.020 to 0.185; $N$ = 1,041), 0.107 (0.036 to 0.178; $N$ = 1,003), and 0.375 (0.307 to 0.444; $N$ = 1,087), which is 5.1, 5.4, and 18.8 percentage points in choosing probability. The Experiment 3 difference is much larger than in Experiments 1 and 2. That experiment also changed task timing, instructions, and face selection; I do not attribute the larger difference to any particular change. No difference in $J$ was detected (estimated differences: 0.009, −0.022, and −0.014; every interval includes zero). The intervals are Welch intervals on participant-level sums, which retain the dependence between a participant's two decisions. This analysis illustrates boundary stability; it does not show that PPB outperforms $c$. With one trial of each type, log-linear $c$ is an affine decreasing function of PPB and yields the same test statistics. Here $J$ is the separation of choosing rates in a binary response, not the confidence-based discriminability that Colloff and Wixted analyzed, so these results do not bear on their conclusions about discriminability. Supplement §8 gives the condition means and the correction algebra.

## Aggregation

A group's bias can be summarized as the mean of the individual indexes or as the index computed from the group's mean rates. An index aggregates exactly when the two coincide; the aggregation discrepancy is the first minus the second. PPB aggregates exactly:

$$\overline{\text{PPB}} = \text{PPB}(\bar{H}, \bar{F})$$ {#eq-aggregation}

@eq-aggregation follows from the linearity of addition. For $c$, the probit transformation is convex above 0.5 and concave below 0.5. Within a region of fixed curvature, Jensen's inequality determines the direction of each rate's contribution to a discrepancy, and the two contributions can cancel. Mean PPB is twice the observers’ mean probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation, regardless of heterogeneity in $d'$. The identity also holds for common observer weights applied to both rates and PPB. Pooled-trial rates equal unweighted observer means only when trial allocations give the same weights; unequal signal and noise counts can weight observers differently. Mean PPB summarizes response propensity, whereas mean $c$ summarizes criterion location under the Gaussian model.

The aggregation discrepancy for PPB was zero to floating-point precision in every configuration. For the other indexes the two summaries are different quantities, and the discrepancy measures how much the choice between them matters. At high accuracy ($\mu_H = 0.90$, $\mu_F = 0.15$), the discrepancy for $c$ reached $-0.059$, nearly half the magnitude of $c$ at the mean rates (@fig-advantages, Panel B). The corresponding discrepancies were $-0.079$ for $B''$, $-0.052$ for $B''_D$, and $+0.033$ for $B_r$. In relative terms, however, the discrepancy represented 6\% of $B_r$ and 48\% of $c$. A common bias or common accuracy is sufficient for exact aggregation of $B_r$, but not necessary: zero covariance between individual $J$ and $B_r$ also suffices (Supplement §3).

Averaging corrected individual values retains their finite-sample bias even when all observers share the same population rates. At $H = 0.95$, $F = 0.20$, and $n = 20$, averaging log-linear-corrected individual values yielded bias of 0.10 in $c$ relative to its population value. Excluding subjects with boundary estimates before averaging increased the bias to 0.22 through selection. PPB required neither correction nor exclusion and remained unbiased when all observations were kept, hence its practical advantage is that it permits the retention of all observations.

## Group comparisons

PPB and $c$ decompose the same two rates along different axes, so groups with similar PPB can differ in $c$ when their accuracy differs. Consider Group A with $H = 0.95$ and $F = 0.08$ and Group B with $H = 0.65$ and $F = 0.40$. Their values of PPB are 1.03 and 1.05, but $J$ is 0.87 and 0.25 and $c$ is $-0.12$ and $-0.07$. PPB ranks Group B as the more liberal, and $c$ ranks Group A as the more liberal. From A to B, $H$ falls by 0.30 and $F$ rises by 0.32, so PPB rises by 0.02, whereas on the probit scale the fall in $H$ outweighs the rise in $F$ because the transformation stretches the scale near 0.95. Matching both $H$ and $F$ would make every index agree. Supplement §7 simulates this comparison with 100 subjects per group and compares groups that share one PPB but differ in the shape of their latent distributions; in the second comparison, the rejection rates of the other indexes follow the difference in $J$.

## Invariance under discriminability manipulations

Snodgrass and Corwin’s ANOVA criteria ask whether an index responds to its intended manipulation without a detected effect of the other manipulation or their interaction. The following statistics are reported in the order PPB, then $c$. In Experiment 1 of Layher et al. [-@layher_who_2020], which crossed faces studied once or five times with three payoff schedules within subjects ($N = 39$), payoffs affected both indexes, while overall memory-strength and interaction effects were not significant: payoff $F(2, 76) = 205.2$ and 166.9, strength $p = .63$ and .95, interaction $p = .20$ and .95. In the Measuring Memory Project [@starns_assessing_2019], which crossed words studied one to three times with bias instructions between subjects ($N = 459$), instructions affected both indexes, while overall memory-strength and interaction effects were not significant: instruction $F(2, 450) = 14.7$ and 13.6, strength $p = .55$ and .15, interaction $p = .20$ and .42. Under the base-rate manipulation of Layher et al., every index failed to meet these criteria, $c$, $J$ and $d'$ included. Raw $J$ also showed payoff and interaction effects in Layher Experiment 1; the Measuring Memory analysis detected a strength effect for $J$ but no instruction or interaction effect (Supplement §1.5).

Non-rejection does not establish invariance. The Layher Experiment 1 conservative-minus-liberal difference in PPB strength effects was 0.066, with a paired 95% interval of [$-0.020$, $0.152$]. In Measuring Memory, the conservative-instruction strength effect on PPB was 0.090, with interval [$0.026$, $0.155$]; the corresponding effect on $c$ was $-0.190$, with interval [$-0.316$, $-0.065$]. Some condition-specific confidence intervals therefore indicate departures from invariance despite the nonsignificant overall tests. Neither dataset replicates the original: Layher et al. used poorly discriminated faces ($d' \le 1.1$) and confounded strength with practice, the Measuring Memory Project induced bias by instruction between subjects, and neither manipulates word imagery.

## Empirical results

At the subject level, 136 of 220 participants (62\%) produced at least one rate equal to 0 or 1 and therefore required a correction for $c$ (@tbl-empirical). At the condition level, 89\% of observations required correction. Among the 136 affected participants, estimates of $c$ under the log-linear and $1/2N$ corrections differed by as much as 0.14. The corrections also differed by as much as 0.15 among interior rates, because the log-linear method adjusts every rate, whereas the $1/2N$ method adjusts only boundary values. PPB remained directly computable for every observation. The denominator of $B_r$ equaled zero ($H = 1$, $F = 0$) for 28 participants (13\%) and 146 of the 440 condition-level observations (33\%).

Boundary estimates were concentrated among participants whose choosing rates most strongly separated trial types. Their prevalence increased across $J$ quartiles: 18\%, 46\%, 83\%, and 100\% (@tbl-quartiles). These are choosing-rate separation quartiles, not quartiles of culprit-identification accuracy.

The value of $c$ computed from mean corrected rates was $-0.1316$, whereas the mean of individual $c$ values was $-0.1418$. The resulting discrepancy was $-0.0102$. These are different criterion summaries; the observed discrepancy was small in absolute units. PPB aggregated exactly under the common participant weights.

### Worked reporting example

Across 880 target-present trials there were 623 perpetrator choices, 95 foil choices, and 162 rejections; across 880 target-absent trials there were 261 foil choices and 619 rejections. Under the stated choosing response, $H=0.8159$, $F=0.2966$, $J=0.5193$, and PPB $=1.1125$. PPB/2 $=0.55625$ is the choosing fraction because the trial types are equally frequent. This descriptive statement needs no latent evidence model.

The point estimates indicated more choosing in own-race lineups (PPB$_{\text{own}} = 1.1341$, PPB$_{\text{other}} = 1.0909$; $c_{\text{own}} = -0.1297$, $c_{\text{other}} = -0.0879$). The paired own-minus-other PPB difference was 0.0432, with a 95% t-based confidence interval of [$-0.0348$, $0.1211$]. Dividing the PPB difference and interval by two gives a choosing-probability difference of 0.0216, with interval [$-0.0174$, $0.0606$]. Thus the direction of the point estimates agrees across PPB and corrected $c$, but the choosing difference is imprecisely estimated. With two trials of each type per condition, log-linear $c$ is an affine decreasing function of PPB, so this agreement is algebraically forced rather than independent evidence of robustness. The estimate based on $c$ depends on corrections for 89\% of the condition-level observations.

The perpetrator-only sensitivity coding gave a pooled sum of 1.0045 instead of 1.1125, reflecting the exclusion of target-present foil choices from the $H$ numerator. Its own-minus-other sum difference was 0.0545 with a 95% paired interval of [$-0.0254$, $0.1345$]. The direction agrees, but the pooled sum cannot be read as twice the observed choosing fraction. The original study estimated the innocent-suspect identification rate by dividing the target-absent choosing rate by lineup size. Neither coding applies that adjustment. Interpreting PPB as suspect-identification bias would therefore require an appropriate lineup model.

# Discussion

PPB revives Macmillan and Creelman's yes rate as the bias index paired with Youden's $J$: its affine transform $(1-\text{PPB})/2$ is the criterion contrast under the centered identity link, and each of its practical advantages follows from that link. In the eyewitness data, $c$ was undefined for 62% of participants. At 10 to 20 trials of each type, boundary corrections introduced bias of up to 0.12 in the tested configurations. In the high-accuracy aggregation simulation, the two group summaries of $c$, the mean of individual values and the value at the mean rates, differed by nearly half the latter’s magnitude. PPB required no correction, and its two summaries coincide. Macmillan and Creelman prefer $c$ to the yes rate for coherence with $d'$ [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 411], but the same principle points to PPB for a researcher who reports $J$, and for bias alone they grant that neither distributional assumption is the stronger (p. 411). They rate the yes rate poorly only on its pairing with a sensitivity index and on its theoretical standing (p. 412).

Hierarchical modeling can support either summary while accounting for participant and item variation [@rouder_introduction_2005; @morey_problematic_2008]. Models of radiologists’ performance already estimate hit and false alarm rates jointly [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007]. PPB is a natural probability-scale summary of fitted hit and false alarm rates, whereas $c$ describes latent criterion location under a supported equal-variance Gaussian model. With common observer weights, PPB at the mean fitted rates equals the mean of individual fitted PPBs; for $c$, those two summaries are different estimands. The reporting target determines which quantity to summarize, while the model determines how variation and dependence are accounted for. PPB can also be computed directly from reported rates when no fitted model is needed. Neither index replaces ROC analysis for comparing discriminability [@mickes_receiver_2012]; PPB summarizes bias at an operating point.

Reporting $H$ and $F$ separately loses nothing, and for a single comparison both should be reported. PPB serves analyses that need one bias number per observer, group, or covariate: ranking or correlating observers, regressing bias on predictors, or testing one contrast, where two rates would otherwise be tested jointly or one of them chosen. The question is which response-bias summary to report alongside $H$ and $F$; this article focuses on the comparison between PPB and $c$.

PPB's advantages matter most under four conditions. Boundary rates are common when observers complete few trials or respond accurately: in eyewitness lineups; in diagnostic mammography, where radiologists each interpreted a median of eight cancers and observed rates reached 100% sensitivity and 0% false positives [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007]; and in truth-discernment tasks, where perfect accuracy leaves $d'$ undefined without an adjustment [@batailler_signal_2022]. When only group-level rates exist, as when each witness is tested once [@mickes_receiver_2012], group PPB can estimate the population mean response sum if the sampling and trial-type allocation identify comparable conditional populations. Raw individual PPB cannot be computed when each witness completes only one trial type. With unequal trial allocations, the weighting of the two rate pools also matters. When rates are modeled on covariates, as for radiologists [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007; @elmore_screening_2002] or for partisan bias in judging news [@batailler_signal_2022], covariate effects on PPB add across the two rate models in probability units. PPB was introduced in such a setting: separate multilevel logistic models for $H$ and $F$ gave covariate-adjusted predicted rates, from which PPB and $J$ were computed with bootstrap intervals, across thousands of respondents judging social ties [@feltham_cognitive_2025]. In large, heterogeneous samples like this, EVSDT is difficult to justify for every observer, whereas PPB's reading as a yes rate needs no distributional assumption.

In practice, report the counts, $H$ and $F$, and pair PPB with $J$. PPB $= 1$ is a descriptive reference point for balanced responding under equal presentation. The response criterion appropriate to a task may depend on signal prevalence and error costs. Use the same participant weights in both rate means and in the mean PPB; the summaries then agree. Give uncertainty at the sampling unit appropriate to the question, using paired differences for repeated conditions. For sparse individual counts, the Clopper--Pearson sum guarantees at least nominal coverage under the binomial model. The adjusted interval is a narrower approximate option that can under-cover in some of the evaluated configurations (Supplement §5). For covariate effects, model $H$ and $F$ separately and sum the predicted rates. Keep observers with boundary rates: excluding them biased $c$ by 0.22 in the follow-up simulation. When reporting $c$, name the correction and check that the conclusions survive the other one, because the two corrections disagree even for interior rates.

$c$ remains the better index when the question concerns latent criterion location and EVSDT has empirical support, as in psychophysical experiments where many trials yield interior rates; boundary corrections then matter less, although differences between average criterion and criterion at mean rates can persist when observers are heterogeneous. It is also the index to use when discriminability is manipulated and the researcher expects observers to hold a criterion fixed on the Gaussian evidence scale, because PPB then varies with $d'$ whenever $c$ differs from zero. The paradigm must justify that expectation. The open datasets did not decide it: the omnibus analyses detected no departures for $c$ under payoffs or instructions, but condition-specific intervals showed departures under conservative instructions. Non-rejection in the omnibus tests does not establish that observers hold either index fixed.

Three limitations remain. First, the attainable range of PPB narrows as accuracy rises, $|J| \le \text{PPB} \le 2-|J|$, so comparisons should report $J$ alongside PPB. $B_r$ normalizes the uncertain region but is undefined at $H=1$, $F=0$. When individual $B_r$ values are defined, $B_r$ at equally weighted mean rates is their weighted average, with weights proportional to $1-J$ (Supplement §3). Second, the empirical boundary illustrations concern choosing in two lineup datasets; they do not validate a suspect-identification criterion. The simulated operating points emphasize boundaries, and the recognition-memory datasets can only partially assess invariance. Third, the guaranteed individual interval is wide, and the narrower adjusted interval has no guarantee (its coverage fell as low as 91.5% on the grid); exact unbiasedness and boundary computability do not remove sampling uncertainty. Participant-level t-based confidence intervals are approximations, and dependence between participants or stimuli requires an analysis that preserves that structure.

Extensions include weighting for unequal presentation probabilities, multiclass and rating-scale data, and suspect-identification models for lineups. The difference $H - F$, Youden's $J$, has served as a distribution-free index of accuracy since @peirce_numerical_1884. PPB is its counterpart for bias, while $c$ remains the index to use when the Gaussian model is (correctly) assumed and the question is criterion location.

: Boundary prevalence and bias indexes by choosing-rate separation quartile in Experiment 1 of Colloff et al. (2022) ($N = 220$). # Open Practices Statement {.unnumbered}

This article reports simulations and secondary analyses of existing datasets; it collects no new participant data. The reanalyses and contrast specifications are exploratory. The supplement gives the estimands, interval construction and sensitivity analyses. The analysis code was developed with AI assistance (see Declarations).

# Data Availability {.unnumbered}

The Colloff et al. data are distributed in the [pyWitness published-data collection](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness/tree/main/data/published/2020_Colloff_Flowe_Smith_etal), which also holds the [Colloff and Wixted data](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness/tree/main/data/published/2020_Colloff_Wixted). The Layher et al. data are available at [OSF project 4k2hb](https://osf.io/4k2hb/), and the Measuring Memory Project data at [OSF project 92ahy](https://osf.io/92ahy/). I do not redistribute these datasets.

# Code Availability {.unnumbered}

The analysis code is available at [github.com/emfeltham/ppb-yes-rate-public](https://github.com/emfeltham/ppb-yes-rate-public), and an included "make" file regenerates every table, figure, and reported value. An R implementation of the PPB confidence intervals is included.

# Declarations {.unnumbered}

**Funding.** This research received no specific funding.

**Conflicts of interest.** The author has no conflicts of interest to declare.

**Ethics approval and consent.** Not applicable. The article reanalyzes publicly available data from published studies; the files contain no names, contact details, or other direct identifiers.

**AI-tool use.** I used AI tools to write and revise the analysis code and to refine the text. I specified the analyses and claims, reviewed all outputs, and take total responsibility for the content.

**Author contributions.** I conceived the study, wrote the code and wrote the manuscript.
